> **Status: experimental.** `chirp()` has been tested on simulated data only.
> Report its calls together with a standard tool such as CellChat.

## 14.1 The problem

Ligand-receptor tools ask whether a ligand is expressed in a sender cluster
and its receptor in a receiver cluster. Most decide "expressed" by detection,
for example the gene seen in at least 10% of a cluster's cells.

Ambient RNA breaks this. If the cell type that dominates the soup makes a
ligand, that ligand is found at low level in every droplet, and every
cluster looks like a sender. Correcting the counts first helps but does not
fully fix it: corrected counts are often small but above zero, so the gene
still counts as detected.

## 14.2 What chirp() does

For each gene and cluster, `chirp()` compares the observed count with the
count ambient RNA is expected to add there:

```
expected ambient[g, k]  =  sum over cells c in k of  rho[c] × total[c] × soup[g]
```

A gene is called in a cluster only if its count is significantly above
`margin` × that expectation (Poisson test, false discovery rate controlled
across genes and clusters). A pair's score is the geometric mean of the
ligand's and receptor's **native** expression: observed minus expected
ambient, per 10,000 of the cluster's own UMIs.

## 14.3 Running it

```r
fit <- decant(counts, empties, clusters = clusters)

pairs <- data.frame(ligand   = c("TGFB1", "CXCL12"),
                    receptor = c("TGFBR1+TGFBR2", "CXCR4"))

res <- chirp(counts, pairs, fit = fit)
res[res$call, ]
```

`counts` must be the **raw** counts, not corrected ones: `chirp()` removes
ambient RNA itself. A subunit complex is written with `+`; it is scored by
its weakest subunit and called only if every subunit is called. Without a
`decant()` fit, pass `soup`, `rho` and `clusters` directly; for several
samples pass a genes × samples `soup` and `sample_of`.

## 14.4 Reading the output

One row per pair × sender × receiver.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `call` | Ligand natively expressed in the sender and receptor in the receiver |
| `score` | Geometric mean of native expression, per 10k |
| `naive_call`, `naive_score` | The same from raw counts with the 10% detection rule, for comparison |
| `ambient_share_ligand` | Share of the ligand's counts in the sender that ambient RNA explains |
| `p_ligand`, `p_receptor` | Adjusted p-values of the two calls |

Rows with `naive_call = TRUE` and `call = FALSE` are links that ambient RNA
alone would have produced. A call whose `ambient_share_ligand` is above
about 0.6 depends heavily on `rho` being right; treat it with caution.

## 14.5 Evidence and limits

On simulated data (2 seeds, contamination 0.05 to 0.3, soup dominated by one
cell type), counting false links between clusters that do not make the
ligand or receptor:

| Method | False links | Strong true links found |
|---|---|---|
| 10% detection rule, raw counts | 608-944 | all |
| `subtract` correction, then detection | 608-944 | all |
| `bayes_cell` correction, then detection | 70-388 | all |
| `chirp()` | 0 | all |

Limits:

- **Simulation only.** The simulator's ambient counts follow the model
  `chirp()` tests against; real data will do worse. CellChat and
  CellPhoneDB, with their own filters, were not run.
- **Weak links are missed.** Pairs whose weaker side is expressed at 5 to 20
  per 10k were found 12 to 36% of the time.
- **It depends on `rho`.** The default `margin = 2` gave no false calls
  with `rho` at two thirds of its true value, but up to 100 at half. Decant's
  estimate has run low on some held-out data
  ([Chapter 12](12-Validation-and-Benchmarks.html)).
- It tests whether the RNA is there, not whether signalling happens, and it
  has no cluster-specificity test.
